headline: Vogglenauts
intro: Vogglenauts is a cozy online co-op game about exploring a tropical world, cleaning up harmful gloop, and solving small mission-based problems together. My part is lead programming: setting up the gameplay architecture, multiplayer patterns, code workflow, and the systems other team members build content on top of.

hero.caption: In-game hub area.

timeline.title: Defining the co-op game loop
timeline.shortText: The game is built around low-stress co-op: players travel through a tropical world, clean up gloop, use different tools, and complete mission objectives together. The programming work has to support that style: readable systems, quick iteration, and multiplayer behavior that does not make simple interactions feel brittle.

media.alt: Vogglenauts beach hub with shared island activities
media.caption: The hub is a shared space before and between missions.

annotations.label: Hub feeling
annotations.detail: The island is meant to work as a friendly shared space instead of a stressful combat arena.

annotations.label: Co-op focus
annotations.detail: The intended play is teamwork, missions, and small shared discoveries.

timeline.outcome: The technical direction is shaped around fast iteration for a cooperative, mission-based game rather than one-off prototype code.

timeline.title: Gameplay code in AngelScript
timeline.shortText: Most gameplay code lives in AngelScript. That gives the team quick iteration: scripts hot-reload on save, even while testing in PIE. I documented the code layout and conventions so gameplay programmers can find the right place for player code, tools, components, missions, enemies, props, and UI.

media.alt: Vogglenauts underwater gameplay with cleanup objectives and player tools
media.caption: Underwater mission gameplay with objectives and tool slots.

annotations.label: Hot reload
annotations.detail: AngelScript keeps gameplay iteration quick because scripts can reload during editor play sessions.

annotations.label: Code layout
annotations.detail: Gameplay code is split into clear folders for player, tool, component, mission, enemy, prop, state, and UI work.

timeline.outcome: The project can keep most moment-to-moment gameplay work in script while still allowing C++ and engine changes when needed.

timeline.title: Tools, components, and missions
timeline.shortText: The tool system is data-driven: tools inherit from a common base and use primary/secondary action configs. Actors expose capabilities through components such as cleanable, buoyant, pickup, glooped, or objective-related components. Missions then query a world subsystem by GameplayTags instead of scanning the whole level.

media.alt: Vogglenauts underwater cleanup mission with objectives
media.caption: Mission gameplay built from tools, components, and objectives.

annotations.label: Tool base
annotations.detail: Shared tool behavior lives in one base class, with configs for different actions.

annotations.label: Mission registry
annotations.detail: Components register with a world subsystem so objectives can find relevant actors by tag.

timeline.outcome: This keeps new content additive: add a component, objective, or tool type without hardcoding every interaction into one large system.

timeline.title: Multiplayer and physics constraints
timeline.shortText: The game uses a listen-server setup with resimulation-based physics. Client-side actions can predict local feedback, but important gameplay state still goes through server validation and multicast updates. The documentation also calls out performance rules: avoid unnecessary Tick work, cache components, budget resimulation actors, and pool projectiles or VFX.

media.caption: Co-op mission spaces need responsive local feedback and server-authoritative state.

annotations.label: Prediction
annotations.detail: Clients can show responsive feedback, then ask the server to validate and replicate the result.

annotations.label: Team workflow
annotations.detail: The technical docs explain conventions so multiple people can work in the same codebase.

timeline.outcome: The multiplayer work is less about one flashy feature and more about making everyday interactions stable enough for co-op play.

timeline.title: Engine fork and team builds
timeline.shortText: The project uses a custom Unreal setup with AngelScript and engine-side changes. I documented how to work with the engine fork, mark local engine modifications, and create UnrealGameSync builds so designers can use precompiled editor binaries instead of building the engine themselves.

media.alt: UnrealGameSync showing Vogglenauts project changelists and sync status
media.caption: UnrealGameSync setup for team builds and project syncing.

annotations.label: Engine changes
annotations.detail: Engine edits are marked clearly so they can be found again during merges and debugging.

annotations.label: UGS builds
annotations.detail: Precompiled editor builds keep non-programmers moving without local engine build times.

timeline.outcome: This is the kind of unglamorous setup work that makes a student team project much easier to keep moving.

closing: Vogglenauts is a good example of the programming work I like: not just making one feature work, but building the systems, conventions, and workflow that let a team keep adding game content without fighting the codebase.
